13.3–13.4 Curvature, the TNB Frame, Velocity and Acceleration

Explanation (added)

Curvature measures how fast the unit tangent turns per unit of distance travelled along the curve, which is why the definition differentiates with respect to arc length and not . The second equality is the Chain Rule, , and the third uses from the arc length function. The last form needs no at all, only and , so it is usually the quickest to compute. In Stewart these are Definition 8, Formula 9 and Theorem 10 of Section 13.3.

“The theorem before” is the result from 13.2 that a vector function of constant length is always orthogonal to its derivative: differentiating gives . So is already perpendicular to the curve's direction, and dividing by its length makes it a unit vector. points toward the side the curve is bending into. This is the length formula for a cross product, (12.4). and are unit vectors at a right angle, so the product has length 1. Together , , are three mutually perpendicular unit vectors that move with the point: the TNB frame.

5The osculating circle

Definition

The circle in the osculating plane through with radius , with centre distance from in the direction of , is the osculating circle: has same curvature and unit tangent and normal vector as .

The last part, after the colon, is in red on the board.

Explanation (added)

A circle of radius has curvature everywhere, so a circle of radius has curvature exactly . Putting its centre on the side makes it bend the same way as the curve and share the curve's tangent line at . In position-vector form the centre is . Sharp bend: large , small circle. Gentle bend: small , large circle.

813.4 Velocity and acceleration

The board heading is “13.4 Velocity + Acceleration”.

Definition

For a space curve we define:

and

and

Explanation (added)

Read as time and as the position of a moving object. Velocity is a vector (it points along the tangent, in the direction of travel); speed is its length, a number, written with no arrow. Speed is also , the same quantity that sits in the bottom of the curvature formula. Going the other way, velocity is an antiderivative of acceleration and position is an antiderivative of velocity, which is what the next two examples use.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • Frame at a point. “Find the unit tangent, unit normal and binormal vectors and the curvature of at the point .” First find the that gives , then follow Section 3: , differentiate, substitute , normalise, cross product.
  • Curvature only. “Find the curvature of ” (use the cross-product formula) or “of at ” (use the plane-curve formula). A follow-up may ask where the curvature is largest.
  • Planes. “Find equations of the normal plane and the osculating plane of the curve at .” Normal vectors are and (or ).
  • Osculating circle. “Find the equation of the osculating circle of at the point ”, as in Section 7: curvature, radius , centre along the normal, then write the circle.
  • Motion from acceleration. “Given , and , find and ”, as in Section 9. Or the forward direction: given , find velocity, speed and acceleration at a time.
  • Projectile. “A projectile is fired with initial speed … at angle of elevation … from height …. Find the position function”, usually followed by when or where it lands, its maximum height, or its speed on impact, all read off the two components of in Section 10.
